exp_design: Based on aerial photographs from 1996 (and in some cases 1984–1985) we selected all forest patches of more than 1 km2. Of these (approximately 40), we selected 15 areas evenly distributed in the elevational range of 1700–2000 m asl. In a similar manner we selected all agricultural areas of more than 1 km2 from aerial photos from 1967, 1975, and 1984–1985. To be considered an agricultural site, the area had to have been in cultivation on the oldest available aerial photo. On the basis of this initial selection we selected 15 sites that were evenly distributed in the area and in the same elevational range as the forest sites. Finally, we selected all stands (around 20) that appeared to be exotic tree plantations (i.e., dense tree cover in an area that in the oldest aerial photos was treeless). In the field we randomly selected one tree in each of the forest sites in an area that was minimally disturbed by humans (selective logging, beehives, coffee production) and >200 m from the forest edge. In the center of the agricultural sites, we selected a mature shade tree in a home garden with coffee (in one site we found no such home garden, hence n = 14). In the plantations we selected a random tree in the middle of the stand. We selected 7 Cupressus-plantations and six Eucalyptus plantations (n = 13 exotic plantations) to get an even distribution between the two plantation types. title: Maize stem borer colonization, establishment and crop damage levels in a maize-leucaena agroforestry system in Kenya
exp_design: Plots were laid out in randomized complete block design, with five replications at Mtwapa and four at Amoyo.
time_raw: The study covered six cropping seasons from October 1992 to August 1995 long rains: April–June, short rains: mid-October–mid-December
T_subpractice_description_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart
T_intercrop_subpractice_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart
T_weed_method_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart
T_residues_subpractice_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart. Plots were mulch with leucaena leaves. During maize planting (at the onset of rains), trees were cut back to 30 cm above ground. Plots were mulched with leucaena leaves, except for one of the 2.25 m plots, and regularly weeded, except for another of the 2.25 m plots.
C_out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Three species of stem-borers were encountered at Mtwapa; Sesamia calamistis, C. partel- lus and Chilo orichalcociliellus. Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994). Fresh pheromone was loaded onto the traps during each moth collection day. Data about the total number of male moths were analysed. Abundance per plot (5 plots per treatment)

title: how natural forest conversion affects insect biodiversity in the peruvian amazon: can agroforestry help?
exp_design: Comparison of 5 land-use systems (natural forest, multistrata agroforest, cocoa agroforest, cassava monoculture, weedy grassland) across several villages near Pucallpa city, Peruvian Amazon. Four sampling plots per village (25 x 25 m); each plot sampled six times with monthly repetition (Macuya forest only four times). Insects collected using one Malaise trap, nine pitfall traps in a 5 x 5 m grid, and sweeping net zigzag transects (80 m) per plot, between 6:30-10:30 am, March-August 2009 and February-November 2010. Per Table 1, not all habitats occur in all villages.
time_raw: March to August 2009, and February to November 2010
C_subpractice_description_raw: primary natural forest (selectively logged 20+ yrs ago; closed canopy; 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade) and ~20 yr old closed-canopy forest in Pimental
T_subpractice_description_raw: Multistrata agroforest: Inga edulis + pineapples, 6 yrs old, tree density 5-7 trees/25 m2, trees 6-9 m high, 75-80% ground shade

exp_design: To control for local effects, study sites were closely situated in a ~25 km² area representing a variety of land uses and management intensities (Fig. S1); distances between capture sites varied from 27 m (within small forest fragments) to 5 km … We treat each night as an independent sample for statistical analyses

C_out_exp_design:
We recorded bats in forest fragments and in coffee plantations 
of differing diversity and density of shade trees; these plantations 
represented the greatest possible range of management intensities 
in the area...recording time was always similar to time spent 
mist-netting at each site (1800 h to 0400 hours in the dry season, 
and 1800 h to 0200 h in the wet season), with recording 
suspended during high winds or heavy rain. We recorded for an

title: Different crop rotation systems as drivers of change in soil bacterial community structure and yield of rice, Oryza sativa

exp_design: Plots were laid out in randomized complete block design, with five replications at Mtwapa and four at Amoyo.
time_raw: The study covered six cropping seasons from October 1992 to August 1995 long rains: April–June, short rains: mid-October–mid-December

C_out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994).
